title: 6 Mind Tricks Scammers Use On Smart People (Ex-Scammer Explains)

lines.text: You think you'd never fall for a scam. Perfect. You're exactly who I wanted. Why?
I'm Lenny. Ex-scammer. And here's a secret from the inside. I never needed you to be stupid. I needed you to be busy, kind, or scared.
People who are sure they'd never fall for it often check less. They trust their gut. And the gut is exactly what I was talking to.
I once had an engineer, a man who designs bridges, read me his bank code because he was late for a meeting. Smart had nothing to do with it. Busy did.
Every scam I ever ran pushed the same six buttons in your brain. Once you can see the buttons, you can switch them off. I'll show you each one, with the exact line I'd use on you.
And at the end, a three question test that catches almost every scam in about five seconds.
Button one. The clock.
Your account will be closed in thirty minutes. This offer ends at midnight. Bail has to be paid today.
Your brain has a fast mode and a slow mode. The slow mode checks things. The fast mode just acts. A deadline flips you into fast mode, and fast mode does what it's told.
That's why I never let you hang up and think. Thinking is slow mode. Slow mode is where I lose.
My favourite trick here was a fake hold. I'd say, let me put you on hold to stop the transfer, and play thirty seconds of music. People on hold don't think. They wait.
Then I'd come back. It's still going through, we have about two minutes. And the clock starts all over again.
Switch it off. Any deadline from a stranger is a reason to slow down, not speed up. Real problems survive ten minutes of checking.

ov.label: SWITCH IT OFF
ov.s: A deadline is a reason to slow down.

lines.text: Button two. The badge.
This is Officer Reynolds from the fraud unit. Your case number is seven four four nine. I'm going to need you to stay on the line.
We're taught from childhood to cooperate with police, banks, doctors, the government. A title, a case number, a calm voice, and people stop asking questions.
The badge doesn't have to be real. It just has to be on the screen, or in the voice. Caller ID can be faked. Logos can be copied. Letters can be printed.
Once I wore a cheap tie on a video call. Just the tie. Nobody ever looked past it.
And when people asked for my badge number, I gave it instantly. A fast answer sounds like a real one.
Switch it off. Authority is something you check, not something you're told. Hang up, find the official number yourself, and call that.

ov.label: SWITCH IT OFF
ov.s: Authority is something you check, not something you're told.

lines.text: Button three. Fear.
Your son's been arrested. Your computer is infected. Your money is being stolen right now. I always opened with the worst thing I could think of.
When you're scared, the thinking part of your brain goes quiet, and the part that wants to fix it right now takes over. A scared engineer is just as easy as anyone else.
Fear is also why we always offered a solution in the same breath. Here's the problem, and luckily, I can fix it. You'd hold onto me like a life jacket.
And fear makes you hide things. People who are scared and ashamed don't call their family. That silence was exactly what I needed.
Switch it off. Notice the fear itself. The moment your heart is pounding over a call or a message, that's the signal to stop and call someone you trust.
Quick one. If you've ever felt one of these buttons get pushed, subscribe. Every week I open up another one of my old scripts.
Button four. The favour.
This one's quiet. I do something nice for you first. I listen. I give advice. I send you a small payment for a task. I let you withdraw a hundred dollars.
Humans are wired to pay back kindness. If someone helped you, saying no to them feels rude. Even when what they ask for is much bigger than what they gave.
It's the oldest rule in my old business. Give a little, then take a lot. The gift always costs less than what comes back.
That's why the easy job scam pays you first. Why the wrong number guy never asks for anything for weeks. The gift is the hook.
In the romance version, the favour is attention. A good morning text every day for a month is a gift. And people want to give something back.
Switch it off. You don't owe a stranger anything for being nice to you. Kindness that comes before a money request isn't kindness. It's a down payment.

ov.label: SWITCH IT OFF
ov.s: Kindness before a money ask is a down payment.

lines.text: Button five. Everyone else is doing it.
Two hundred people in the group chat posting their profits. Five star reviews. A counter on the website. Three thousand people joined today. Testimonials with photos.
When you're not sure what to do, you look at what other people are doing. So I built you a crowd. Every one of those people was me, or someone I paid, or a bot.
Fake reviews are cheap. Fake followers are cheap. A crowd costs me almost nothing, and it does my convincing for me.
We even faked the people who doubted. Someone in the chat would say, I didn't believe it at first, and I missed out. Regret is a powerful crowd.
Switch it off. A crowd inside their app, their chat, or their website proves nothing. Look for what independent people say, somewhere they don't control.
And button six. The small yes.
I never asked for your savings first. I asked for a reply. Then a name. Then two dollars. Then two hundred. Each yes made the next one easier.
And once you've put money in, a second trap closes. Walking away means admitting the first payment was lost. So you pay the fee to save the money. Then another fee.
That's why so many people lose more after they start to suspect something. Stopping feels like losing. Paying one more time feels like hope.
In my old crew, we had a name for the moment someone sent their first real amount. We said, they're in. After that, the job was just keeping them in.
Switch it off. Ask, if I'd known on day one where this would end, would I have started? And remember, money you've already lost is gone either way. Don't send more after it.

ov.label: SWITCH IT OFF
ov.s: Don't send good money after lost money.

lines.text: Now, the real trick. I never pushed just one button. I pushed three or four at once.
The bank call. That's the badge, the clock and fear in one sentence. This is your bank's fraud team, your money is leaving your account right now.
The wrong number scam. That's the favour, the crowd, and the small yes, slowly, over weeks. Different speed, same buttons.
So you don't need to memorise every scam out there. There will be new ones every month. You only need to recognise the buttons.
There are scams I never heard of that will exist next year. New apps, new AI tricks, new excuses. Same six buttons. Every time.
So here's the test. Three questions. Five seconds.
One. Did they contact me, or did I contact them? Scams almost always start with them reaching out.
Two. Is it about money, a code, a password, or access to my device?
Three. Am I being rushed, scared, or flattered right now?
You don't need all three. Most scams hit two of them in the very first message. The good ones hit all three before you've finished reading.
If the answer is yes to two of those, stop. Don't argue with them. Don't try to outsmart them. Just leave the conversation, and check it yourself, through a number or app you already trust.
That's honestly the thing I feared most back then. Not police. Not smart people. People who just said, I'll call you back, and actually did it, on a real number.
And if they argue, push, or get angry when you say you'll call back? That's your answer. A real bank is happy for you to check.
And if you ever do fall for one, you're not stupid. You're human. These scripts are written by people who do this all day, every day, and test what works on thousands of people.
The people who get hurt most are the ones who are too ashamed to tell anyone. So tell someone. Call your bank. Report it. The faster, the better.
And if it happened to someone you love, don't say how could you. Say, thank you for telling me. That sentence is how they tell you next time too.
Quick recap. The clock. The badge. Fear. The favour. Everyone else. And the small yes.
Which button gets you? Be honest. Tell me in the comments. Mine was always the favour. That's how I got recruited in the first place.
And if you can't pick one, it's probably the clock. Busy people were always my favourite people. No offence.
And send this to the smartest person you know. They're the one who thinks they don't need it.
Trust me. I pushed all six.
